inline.s: Ma Danyang said:

One who studies the Way must empty his heart and lower his tone, and not be ashamed to ask of those beneath him; only then does he gain one step and go on to the next, each step higher than the last. Thread by thread he gathers, and it becomes a foot; foot upon foot, and it becomes a yard; yard upon yard, and it becomes a fathom. Ten makes a hundred, a hundred makes a thousand, a thousand makes ten thousand. Yet the wonder of the Way is not reckoned by numbers, and so it is said that the wonder of the Way is without limit. You have now gained a little of the mysterious work, and you think the Way ends there. Every month you cling to this house of yours, sitting withered in ashen despondency, understanding neither the principle of yin and yang nor the workings of creation, and never going before your master to seek instruction. Held back by the difference between man and woman, you have raised up the view of self and other. When the master saw you dead-set in this method, unable ever to finish the Way, he wished to come in person and instruct you; but he too was hindered by the risk of scandal, and therefore his yang spirit appeared, dividing its body to save and convert you.

The master has told me again and again: 'One yin and one yang, that is called the Way; apart from yin and yang the Way cannot be completed.' This yin and yang is the yin and yang of the yang fire and the yin tally. It does not mean the yin and yang of men marrying and women taking husbands, of ordering the world. 'This' speaks of so wondrous a principle, and it is a pity you do not awaken to it. 'That' speaks of such a mystery, and I sigh that you do not know it. 'The lone yang does not grow': yang belongs to fire, and when fire is excessive it must grow feverish, and the elixir cannot be formed. 'The orphaned yin does not arise': yin gives birth to water, and when water is excessive it must overflow, and the elixir cannot be formed. This 'orphaned yin and lone yang' is a figure for water and fire that cannot aid each other.

In sum, one who cultivates the Way must have water and fire aiding each other and yin and yang running through, and only then can the elixir be returned. When he says you 'have turned your back on the furnace of creation,' he is plainly telling you that you do not understand the principle of true yin and true yang. 'The grown man and the complaining maiden' also means 'the orphaned yin does not arise, the lone yang does not grow.' So he plainly tells you that one who studies the Way cannot be without this yin and yang. This yin and yang is the wondrous function of returning the elixir. The 'yellow dame' is true intent. To join yin and yang through true intent is like lifting the jug and urging a man to drink fine wine (
liáng yùn

, good wine). True intent belongs to earth, and earth encloses yellow, and so she is figured as a dame. The maiden of the Western House is metal; metal flourishes in the west, and so she is called the Western House. The young man of the Eastern House is wood; wood flourishes in the east, and so it is said that 'east and west match each other.' 'Two and eight' is the number of one catty. Metal cannot be subdued unless it is the child of wood, and wood cannot be born unless it is the child of metal; this is the principle of yin and yang, creation, and the mutual overcoming of the five phases.

One who cultivates the Way must join them through intent, like a matchmaker reconciling two houses, so that metal and wood meet, with nothing between them, like the love of husband and wife. The 'bridal chamber' is the elixir court; it brings metal and wood home to the elixir court. 'Metal' is the corporeal soul; 'wood' is the ethereal soul. Gather these two souls in one place, clinging and unwilling to part, leaning one upon the other: the ethereal soul does not leave the corporeal soul, the corporeal soul does not leave the ethereal soul, like husband and wife, the two matching each other. Quicksilver is eight ounces, and lead is eight ounces as well. 'Mutual response' is where the elixir is formed. It means that the two souls lean upon each other; when essence and qi seem to respond, they congeal within, as in conception. 'Ten months' means the number is complete. 'Warm nourishment' is the firing times. This speaks of essence and qi congealing and being refined by the firing times into the elixir. 'Full' means perfect and complete: when the work is perfect and complete, the infant is born. The 'infant' is the spirit transformed from true qi. When this spirit comes forth from the Mud Pill Palace, ascends to pay court at the Golden Gate, and becomes a realized man, is that not to be an immortal?"
When Danyang had finished speaking, Bu'er was greatly awakened. If you would know what happened afterward, read the next chapter.
Yin and yang in harmony, true intent runs through; / bodhi's clear light, the mind's own traces, view;
Would you in the Pure Land seek the mystery through? / The Way lies with the master, the practice with you.

blocks.text: 10. Preaching the Three Vehicles, He Expounds the Way of Complete Truth; Ruining Her Countenance, She Gladly Becomes an Ugly Woman

inline.s: Once the true transmission is won, the Way may be plied; / the three vehicles' wondrous Dharma waits for you to decide.
That day Yuanzhen marred her own face, you recall, / to gain a golden body through ten thousand autumns' fall.

The story tells that when Sun Bu'er heard Ma Danyang's words they fell on her like a blow to the head, shattering the net of her delusion and bringing her to sudden awakening, as though she had started from a dream. She sighed and said, "Had it not been for your words, Elder Brother, I would nearly have ruined the great matter. Ordinarily I am a little quicker of understanding than you, Elder Brother; so why, once I took up the study of the Way, am I not your equal?" Ma Danyang said, "It is not that you are not my equal; it is only that you would not go and seek instruction, and so you are not my equal. Hence the saying, 'The clever are undone by their own cleverness; many a clever man has undone himself.' In the affairs of the world, only learning brings knowledge. How many are born knowing?" Sun Bu'er thanked him, saying, "I shall reverently obey the master's instruction, and from today I shall humbly seek teaching." Ma Danyang was greatly pleased, and went back to the side rooms by himself. Several days passed, and he had to go to his maternal uncle's house to offer birthday congratulations. He prepared all the gifts, explained the matter to the master, and invited Sun Bu'er to go with him. Sun Bu'er pleaded illness and would not go, so Ma Danyang had no choice but to order a servant boy to carry the gifts, and mounting his black donkey he set off for his uncle's house.

Leaving Danyang's journey aside, let us speak of Sun Bu'er in her room. Because Ma Danyang had said she would not seek instruction, and so did not understand the wonder of the Way, she took it to heart. Now, seeing that Ma Danyang was not at home and that all the servants, men and women, were at play in the front, she went alone to the thatched hut. Seeing the master sitting cross-legged in meditation, she knelt before him and said, "This disciple Sun Bu'er is dull of nature and does not understand the highest principle, and so has twice gone astray. Yesterday, thanks to Elder Brother's instruction, I learned that what you spoke before was the Way, and I repent it too late. I beg the master to pardon me and instruct me once more." So saying, she knocked her head several times without pause. Master Wang Chongyang said, "Stand up, and I will speak with you. The Way has three vehicles; one acts according to his measure. Now I will expound them for you, and we shall see which vehicle you can study." Then Sun Bu'er rose and stood to one side, bowing as she listened to the teaching.
Master Chongyang said:
One who studies the Way must set life and death beyond his concern; if he can break through this one word 'death,' he may become a man who does not die.

The highest vehicle is the Way of emptiness and nothingness. Not one thread hanging, not one speck of dust clinging, like the bright moon in an empty sky with not a cloud for ten thousand li. Only a single point of the spirit-root, and one can seize the creation of heaven and earth and fathom the true principle of yin and yang. Refine it by the method, and one can make the existent return to nothingness and from nothingness give birth again to the existent. One may grow old together with heaven and earth and cultivate as long as the sun and moon: this is the Way of the highest grade of celestial immortals.

The middle vehicle is to keep the precepts with reverent sincerity, to serve the sages and the true with worship, to recite the holy names of the Heavenly Worthy and to intone the secret writings of the Most High. When a single thought is pure and true, ten thousand cares are all made clear; one reaches up to the azure vault, and all spirits see into one, and the light of the spirit is not extinguished. A single point of true nature goes straight through to emptiness and nothingness, and one takes rank among the immortals: this is the Way of the middle vehicle.

As for the lowest vehicle, it is to pile up merit and accumulate practice. Widely practice skillful means, aid men and benefit beings; do many good deeds and constantly examine one's own faults. Then the true nature will not be darkened, and the spiritual brightness can of itself shine forth. Now hidden, now manifest, no different from an immortal: this is the Way of the lowest vehicle.
Weigh your own strength: which vehicle do you wish to study? I shall transmit to you the true method."
Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple wishes to study the highest vehicle, the Way of celestial immortals."

Master Chongyang laughed and said, "Your heart is large indeed, but I fear your resolve is not firm." Sun Bu'er said, "My heart is not large, but my resolve is very firm. This body can be destroyed, but my resolve cannot be taken from me." Master Chongyang said, "Whoever cultivates the Way must obtain the spiritual power of mountains and rivers, and so the lay of the land must be chosen. Now in Luoyang of the Eastern Commandery the spiritual power is at its height, and a true immortal ought to appear there. If you go to that place and cultivate for twelve years, you may hope to accomplish the Way. Can you go?" Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple is willing to go."

Master Chongyang looked at her once, shook his head, and said, "You cannot go! You cannot go!" Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple would cast aside life and forget death; why can I not go?" Master Chongyang said, "If one dies, one must die to some purpose. If you die to no purpose, have you not thrown your life away for nothing? Luoyang is a thousand li from here, and along the road there are many gallants and wandering blades, and very many frivolous young men. If they see that your face is like a flower and your looks like jade, how would their hearts not be stirred? At the least they will speak wild words in jest, and at the worst they will surely offer you insult. Yours is a nature of chastity and ardor; how could you bear their foul defilement? You would certainly stake your life to preserve your name and honor. You meant to seek long life, and would instead lose your life. That is why I say you cannot go."

When Sun Bu'er heard this she pondered for a long while. Without taking leave of the master, she left the thatched hut and went to the kitchen, where she sent away everyone who did the cooking. With her own hands she lit the fire and poured a whole jar of clear oil into the pan. When the oil was boiling, she took a bowl of cold water in her hand, turned her face toward the pan, shut both eyes tight, steeled her heart, and poured the cold water into the pan. The boiling oil, meeting the cold water as it burst in, spattered oil drops all over her face, and everywhere the drops fell they were scalded into blisters. Enduring the pain, Sun Bu'er came to see the master and said, "In this state, master, may I go?" At the sight of her Master Chongyang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Wonderful! Wonderful! That the world should hold a person of such great resolve; my journey to Shandong was not made in vain." Having spoken, the master at once transmitted to Sun Bu'er the whole of the wondrous principle of yin and yang, the mysterious workings of creation, and the work of refining yin into yang and transcending the ordinary to enter sagehood.

When the transmission was done, he said, "The great Way is hidden in not knowing and not recognizing. This work of not knowing and not recognizing must wait upon a touch of madness before it can be concealed from others, so that they do not know that I have this work, nor recognize that I am practicing. Only on the day the great work is accomplished may one appear in person to preach the Dharma. Wait until the oil blisters on your face have healed, then go quickly to Luoyang. There is no need to come and take leave of me; when your merit is round and your fruit is full, we shall meet again at the Peach Banquet."

When the master had finished speaking, he closed his eyes and said no more. Sun Bu'er bowed to the master several times and left the thatched hut. She saw the serving women and maids come in from outside, and meeting her head-on they were startled out of their wits. Had she not worn her usual clothes, they would scarcely have known her. They all came at once to ask, "What is the reason for this?" Sun Bu'er said, "I wanted to make a few fried cakes for old Mr. Chongyang, and feared that you were not clean, so I sent you all away. Working with my own hands, I carelessly poured cold water into the boiling oil, and could not dodge in time, and so my whole face was scalded into blisters. This is a passing calamity of mine, nothing very serious; you need not be alarmed. Go about your proper business, each of you, and do not let me be on your minds." Having spoken, she went back to her inner room, shut the door, and silently took up the work the master had transmitted, doing it one item at a time. The oral instructions and wondrous words she rehearsed anew.

Two days later Danyang returned. As he was about to enter the gate, the serving women told him that Sun Bu'er's face had been scalded by boiling oil. Ma Danyang sighed without end. He first went to the thatched hut and paid his respects to the master, then came to the main chamber to see Sun Bu'er. He saw that her whole face was covered with blisters, and that the blisters had already festered and burst, with yellow fluid running in streams, turning a face like a flower and jade into the visage of a ghost. At the sight Ma Danyang could not but groan, and he called out, "Fellow cultivator Sun, why were you not careful, that the oil scalded you into this state? How you have suffered!"

Before he had finished speaking, Sun Bu'er opened her eyes wide, looked at Ma Danyang, and laughed without stopping. She stepped forward, seized Ma Danyang with one hand, and said, "Are you a boy of the Queen Mother of the West? She has sent you to invite me to the Peach Banquet; today I shall go with you to the heavenly palace. Hurry! Hurry!" So saying, she climbed up on the table, clutched at the window lattice with her hands, and made as if to rise into the air. Suddenly she fell with a thump, lay on the ground, and moaned without ceasing.

Ma Danyang hastily helped her up, but she wept and laughed by turns. Seeing her in such a state, Ma Danyang felt a certain desolation in his heart, and went again to the thatched hut to see the master, saying, "My fellow cultivator Sun has gone mad with longing for immortality; what is to be done?" Master Chongyang said, "If one is not mad and not addled, who would become an immortal?" When Ma Danyang would have questioned him further, the master had already closed his eyes and entered stillness, and paid him no heed at all. Seeing that the master would not answer, Ma Danyang had no choice but to leave the thatched hut and return to the front hall, dejected and joyless.

Let us tell again how Sun Bu'er, with a few mad words, sent Danyang away, and so won quiet and stillness for herself, exactly right for the work. She worked until her nature-substance was round and bright, a wonder beyond words. When her mind ground grew clear, she first understood how many benefits there are in pursuing the Way, and was exceedingly glad. She took up a mottled-bronze mirror and looked at herself, and was startled. She saw her whole face scarred, red and black in patches, and having gone more than a month without combing her hair or dressing, her hair was a tangled mass, like a shaggy-haired ghoul; in truth a Kumbhanda, a living yaksha. In no way did she look like a squire's wife. When Sun Bu'er had studied her own appearance, she was overjoyed within, and said to herself that now she could go to Luoyang.

So she tore her clothes into tatters at random, smeared a handful of soot from the pan over her face, ran out before the hall, and laughed three times aloud. At once she startled all those maids and serving girls, the household servants and the young lads, who all came together and surrounded her. When Sun Bu'er saw them press close, she made to go out. The maids came to pull her back, and Sun Bu'er bit about her with her mouth. There was one maid who was closest to her; she clutched at Sun Bu'er's clothes and would not let go, and Sun Bu'er turned her head and bit her hand so hard that it bled. The maid let go her hand, and Sun Bu'er was already gone. The serving women and maids, seeing how fierce she was, dared not pull her back, and hurried to report it to the squire. Now it is told that Ma Danyang was sitting in meditation in the side room when he suddenly heard a clamor outside. He rose quickly from his seat and came out to look, and saw the servants come and report, "Madam Sun has gone violently mad and has run out of the house." When Ma Danyang heard this, he feared some mishap, and urgently ordered the servants to give chase at once, while he himself came after them.

Now Sun Bu'er walked straight out of the estate, and the men who kept the gate could not stop her. The people before and behind the estate did not recognize her at once as Madam Sun, and so she got away. Sun Bu'er knew that someone would surely come after her. Seeing a heap of wild brush beyond the village, she plunged into it. Sure enough, Ma Danyang came up with the servants and lads, the women and maids, all in pursuit; they went on ahead for a while, then suddenly turned back and went off again by the way they had come.

Sun Bu'er saw it all clearly from the brush, and only when they had gone far did she come out and set off toward the southwest. By day she begged in the villages, by night she lodged in old temples, always in desolate, secluded, uninhabited places: great trees, sheer cliffs, any spot that could keep off the rain. If anyone came to ask her questions, she gave one line about heaven and one about earth, raving and babbling, weeping and laughing. Seeing her in this state, people knew she was a madwoman and asked her no more. And so all along the road she went safe and sound, and when she met men of upright conduct she would ask the way. In less than two months she reached Luoyang. Whether she truly could accomplish the Way and become an immortal, read the next chapter to learn.
A single leaf of a boat roams the great sea; / the ten-thousand-fathom waves bring no alarm to me.

blocks.text: 11. Hail Falls, and Heaven's Lord Protects the Dharma; Wondrous Reckoning Is Cast, and the Realized Man Points Out the Way

inline.s: Long years mired and sunk in the drowning tide, / where the river of craving rolls, its billows sky-wide;
Cultivate, and you may climb the farther shore; / why seek another boat in midstream any more?

The story tells that after Sun Bu'er left Ma Family Estate she feigned madness all along the road. She traveled several months and came to the outskirts of Luoyang, where there was a broken tile kiln, and there she took shelter. She often went into the county town to beg for food, playing the madwoman to the utmost. She set the little children trailing after her in a pack, crying, "There goes the madwoman, long and short!" and so they made her name known. Inside and outside the town and countryside everyone knew her for a madwoman, and no one came to trouble her any more. Thus she could set her mind at ease and awaken to the Way, which matched Master Chongyang's words, "The great Way is hidden in madness."

It is further told that in Luoyang county there were two notorious ruffians, one named Zhang San and one named Li Si, who were forever lewd and swindling and stopped at nothing. They had often seen Sun Bu'er begging in the streets; ugly as her face was, her eyes were bright and her teeth white, and but for the many scars on her face her looks would not have been poor. These two ruffians took note of her with their eyes and laid it up in their hearts. That night the moon was white and the breeze clear, the sky full of stars, and the two were coming back from the countryside, where they had cheated honest folk. Mellow with drink, they came to a place not far from the broken tile kiln, and Zhang San said, "Let us go and amuse ourselves with that madwoman!" Li Si said, "Do not go, do not go. I have heard tell that if a man lies with a madwoman he is unlucky all his life and never has any long run of fortune." Zhang San said, "We are men whom the gods of heaven will not take in and the gods of earth will not want; what do we care for a long run of fortune or no?" So he would not listen to Li Si, and went on straight toward the broken tile kiln, and Li Si had no choice but to follow him on ahead. They had not gone many steps when suddenly they saw a black cloud overhead, close by the kiln, and with a sudden crack of thunder, as if the mountains were falling and the earth splitting, it burst above their heads and shook Zhang San and Li Si until they trembled in every limb.

That black cloud scattered in an instant, and heaven and earth went dark, so that a man could not see his own hand. A wild wind sprang up and blew through the two of them until the cold pierced their bones. Then a fierce rain came down, drumming on their heads like a war drum, until their heads swam and ached. Li Si put up his hand to shield his skull, and the rain struck the back of his hand like iron pellets, and only then did he know it was not rain; it was hail, which men call snow-pellets, and in common speech cold ones. The cold ones beat the two of them until they had nowhere to turn and no place to hide. Li Si said without ceasing, "A living retribution! I said we should not come, and you would come by force; now let us see how it goes." When Zhang San heard Li Si reproaching him, he grew angry, and all at once his foot came down on a hailstone. The hailstone was smooth and slippery, and how could a foot stand firm on it? He slid and fell flat, scrambled up in a flurry, and stepped once more on empty air and fell flat again, as though someone were pushing him. He stumbled again and again, until his head was cut and his eyes swollen, his flesh mangled and his blood running, and he could only cry out to heaven.

Before long the clouds parted and the moon appeared, and the sky was full of stars again. Li Si had taken a few cold ones, but he never stumbled or fell, and so came to no great harm; only Zhang San, after those falls, was dizzy and dim-sighted, and could only put out his tongue, shake his head, and say, "This will never do! This will never do! That madwoman is not to be trifled with!" Li Si said, "Only now do you know she is not to be trifled with; let us see whether you will come again next time!" Talking as they went, the two made their way home. Li Si told the whole story to those vagabonds and ruffians; one man told ten, and ten told a hundred, and so those who would not learn to be good, and the beggars too, never dared come to the broken tile kiln again. Sun Bu'er stayed in Luoyang twelve years, cultivating and awakening to the Way, and never once did a wicked man trouble her; all of it was thanks to Li Si. Later readers, coming to this place in the book, have a poem that sighs:
Here the realized man awakened to the mysterious work; / how could a mad ruffian come to play the bravo's part?
When the hail came down and he took his beating sore, / he learned that Heaven's Lord protects the Dharma evermore.

Master Wang Chongyang had been in Squire Ma's house more than a year without his noticing it. Out in the village a few old men were idly talking, and said, "Squire Ma does not know how to enjoy his good fortune. He has simply given away a whole family estate to an outsider, and driven his wife out of her wits; no one knows where she has gone." Among them was a man of fifty-odd years named Duan Anren, who said:

Yesterday I went to his estate to visit Squire Ma. There was no one keeping watch at the gate. When I went in, I did not see a single woman; there were only men. I asked where the squire was, and they told me, 'He is behind, in the thatched hut, listening to Master Chongyang preach the Way.' So I walked on back, and saw many thatched huts built there, with Squire Ma and Wang Chongyang sitting in meditation in the one in the middle. When Squire Ma saw me he came out at once and accompanied me to the front hall to talk. I asked him where his wife had gone, and Squire Ma said, 'She has her Way, and I have my wonder.' I asked again, 'Why do I not see the maids and serving girls?' The squire said, 'The men I have married off, the women I have married out; each has set up a household of his own, and there is no tie left to fret over.' I asked again, 'What are these thatched huts built for?' The squire said, 'To gather those who cultivate the Way, that they may awaken to the Way and nourish the true nature.' I asked again, 'Why does Master Chongyang never come out?' The squire said, 'He loves quiet above all things, and does not mix with worldly folk.' When I had asked my questions, I took leave of the squire and came away.

I met Ma Xing, and I put my questions to him as well. 'This estate of yours was so lively before; why is it so cold and still now, like a monastery?' Ma Xing said, 'You do not know. This Master Chongyang who has come to our house is a living immortal. He does not care for bustle; what he loves is quiet. Since Madam Sun left, he has sent away all the maids and serving women and menservants in the estate, and kept only a few of us old faithful ones to watch over the place; that is why it is so still.' I asked Ma Xing again, how he knew that Master Chongyang was a living immortal. Ma Xing answered me, 'In all the affairs of the household, and all that happened in former days, there is nothing anyone has to tell him; he knows it all. Is that not strange? And there are things still to come, and which day will be fair and which day rainy; there is nothing he does not know. Is he not a living immortal?'"

When Duan Anren had finished all he had to say about Ma Family Estate, one of the village elders, an old man of the Pan family, said, "By what you say, he knows things past and things to come. We have had this drought a long while and no rain has fallen; why do we not all go and ask him when the rain will come?" The village elders said with one voice, "Good!" So they came with Old Pan to Ma Family Estate. First they saw Squire Ma and explained their errand, and Ma Danyang led the elders to the thatched hut to ask Master Chongyang, "When will it rain?" The master said, "On the wall of the Earth God's shrine at the east end of your village, the date of the rain is written; go and look, and you will know." When the village elders heard this they came out of the estate at once, went back to their own village, and made their way to the east end. Arriving before the Earth God's shrine, they indeed saw several lines of writing on the whitewashed wall.

Old Pan read it out to the company: "Before the King of Men a pair of melons stands; a pearl shines upon the King's own lands; on the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends; from the monk's mouth mud comes forth from his hands." Below, in small characters, were written the words "Four Characters Unriddled." When Old Pan had read it he laughed and said, "This is a character riddle some schoolboy wrote here; what has it to do with the date of rain?" The village elders asked, "What character riddle is it? Can you guess it?" Old Pan said, "I am used to character riddles. How could I not guess it?" The village elders said, "Since you can guess it, guess it quickly and let us hear." Old Pan said, "Add a few drops of rain to the King of Men and you have the character for gold. Add one dot beside the character for king and you have the character for jade. 'On the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends' - fit the pieces together (join and gather them into one) and you have the character for full. From the monk take away the character for 'monk' and keep 'shang.' Mud is earth. Put 'shang' on top of earth - is that not the character for hall? Plainly it is the four characters 'gold and jade fill the hall.' Where is any date for rain in that?"

Duan Anren stepped forward, pointed with his finger at the line "on the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends," and said, "This is plainly the date of the rain, and you insist there is none. Though these are but a few dumb riddles, there is a hidden juncture in them. Today is the nineteenth; from the twenty-third it is only four days. Let us see whether there is rain on the twenty-third, and then we shall know whether he is efficacious or not." The village elders all said, "What you say is reasonable." So they went home, each to his own house. When the twenty-third day came, black clouds filled the sky and the rain poured down in torrents, from morning until noon, and only then did it stop. Only then did the villagers believe that Master Chongyang was a spirit.

There was also a man of the northern village who lost a cow; he searched everywhere and could not find it, and came to ask the master. Master Chongyang said, "The cow is in the southern village, up in a great tree, in a magpie's nest." When the man who had lost the cow heard this he could not help laughing, and said, "A cow that size, and a magpie's nest that tiny, how could it fit?" Master Chongyang said, "Go, and you will get your cow; say no more." The man had no choice but to leave the thatched hut and come to the southern village, where indeed he saw a very tall tree with a magpie's nest in it. Country folk know how to climb trees, so he climbed up to take the nest, and found it an empty one. He pulled at it with his hand, and a dead branch fell and struck him in the face. As he bowed his head a little, he saw a cow tethered inside a broken house in the village. Looking closely, it was the very cow he had lost. The cow was lying in the broken house with firewood and straw piled outside it and covered over on every side; had he not looked down from a height, he could never have seen it. The man hurried down from the tree, understanding in his heart that there had long been a gentleman on the roof in that village who was used to such work. Had the master not pointed the way, by nightfall the thief would have led the cow far off and sold it to someone else, and it could never have been found again. The man went into the broken house and led his cow home.

Of this we say no more. That day several people from the western village came with questions of their own. Among them was a boy of thirteen or fourteen, who said that his elder brother had been gone from home several months and he did not know when he would return, and so he had come to ask old Master Chongyang. Chongyang said, "Go home and ask your mother's hand." When the boy heard this he laughed without stopping. A little later he came home and saw his mother holding a letter in her hand, and she said, "Your elder brother is in business in Laizhou and has sent a letter back. The man who brought it has just gone; open the letter and read it to me." The boy opened the letter and read: "From your unworthy son, a letter offered to my kind mother. Since father's passing, I have been raised to manhood by your care. Now I carry out my father's purpose and engage in trade abroad, and things have gone fairly well. At present my accounts are not all collected, and I cannot return quickly to comfort my mother's heart. When the autumn cools, I shall come home in the middle of the ninth month to attend upon you with sweet dainties (fine foods)." The boy had not finished reading when he clapped his hands and laughed aloud, saying, "How efficacious! How efficacious!" His mother was just about to question him when she saw five or six men come to the gate; what they wanted, read the next chapter to learn.
But for the fisherman to lead the way, / how could one ever meet the waves?

blocks.text: 12. Pointing Out the Sitting Work, He Sets Forth the Wondrous Principle; Studying the True Way, He Joyfully Meets an Enlightened Master

inline.s: Love and kindness bind and tangle, past all untying; / when the day comes to go, none goes with you in your dying.
Now let your hands fall free, with nothing clinging fast, / and mount straight to the Jade Pool's white jade stair at last.

The story tells that the boy of the western village was just about to tell his mother what Master Chongyang had said about asking her hand, when suddenly he saw five or six men come to the gate and ask which road led to Ma Family Estate. The boy said, "You ask the way to Ma Family Estate; are you by chance going to see the living immortal?" Those men answered, "Just so." When the boy heard that they meant to see the living immortal, he was beside himself with delight, and said to them, "It is not far, not far; I will lead you there." So saying, he went on ahead. The company followed him out of the western village, and before long they came to Ma Family Estate. It was fated that they should have the affinity, for they happened to find Squire Ma sitting before the hall. Seeing them come in, he rose and welcomed them into the hall to be seated, and asked, "What brings you gentlemen to my humble estate?" The several men said, "We have come to seek the Way." When Ma Danyang heard this, he led them to the thatched hut to pay their respects to the master.

Among them was one surnamed Tan, named Chuduan, whose style was Changzhenzi. In former years he had been afflicted with a grave illness, and when Wang Chongyang first came to Shandong he had taught him the work of driving off sickness. Once well, he had set his whole mind on awakening to the Way, and had sought the master everywhere without finding a trace of him. Now he heard men say that a living immortal named Wang Chongyang had appeared at Ma Family Estate, and so he knew the master was here. He had also brought along a fellow seeker of the Way, surnamed Hao, named Datong, whose style was Taigu, a man of Wending county in this same prefecture. The other men too were seekers of the good; there is no need to record their names.

At once Tan Changzhen thanked the master for the kindness of his former healing, and then spoke of his wish to study the Way today. Master Chongyang said, "The Dharma-gate stands wide open: those who go, go; those who come, come; I hold back none who leave, and refuse none who come." He at once ordered Ma Danyang to send them to the second thatched hut to lodge. Some days later two more cultivators arrived: one surnamed Liu, named Chuxuan, whose style was Changshengzi, and one surnamed Wang, named Chuyi, whose style was Yuyangzi, both men of Shandong. Ma Danyang received them, asked their purpose, and found that they too had come to seek the Way, so he led the two of them to the thatched hut to pay their respects to the master. Master Chongyang ordered Ma Danyang to settle them in the third thatched hut. And so one came from the east and one from the west, and in less than a month several dozen had come. Master Chongyang had Ma Danyang agree with them on duties, each to manage one matter, with rules for all, and none might overstep his bounds (overstep his office without leave). When everything was settled, Master Chongyang discoursed with them on the sitting work. The disciples ranged themselves in two rows, bowed, and listened to the teaching.

Man's life has qi for its root, breath for its leader, the heart for its foundation, and the kidneys for its stem. Heaven and earth are eighty-four thousand li apart, and in man the heart and kidneys are eight inches and four tenths apart. The kidneys are the inner kidneys, three inches and three tenths below the navel. A single vessel runs straight through them, to give passage to the breath. The breath governs the hundred vessels: with one exhalation the hundred vessels all open, with one inhalation the hundred vessels all close. The creation of heaven and earth in its ceaseless movement is nothing other than these two words, exhalation and inhalation. If a man's breathing stays always between heart and kidneys, then the blood and qi will of themselves be smooth, the original qi will of itself be firm, the seven emotions will not blaze up, and the hundred illnesses will vanish without being treated.

As for the method of sitting meditation, at each of the hours zi, wu, mao, and you, spread a thick sitting mat in a quiet room. Sit cross-legged on the mat, with the eyes slightly open and looking toward the navel. Stop the ears with cotton, and let the mind cut off all thoughts and cares. Let the intent follow the breath, going and coming, rising and falling with the breath, neither too slow nor too fast, letting it be natural. After sitting the time of one stick of incense, you will find the breath at mouth and nose no longer coarse, but gradually soft and fine. After another stick of incense, you will find the breath at mouth and nose as though present and as though not. Then slowly stretch out the legs and open the eyes, take out the earplugs, and leave the seat to walk a few steps. Then lie down on your side for a while, and when you rise, sip half a bowl of congee broth. You must not do heavy work, and above all must not give way to anger, lest it spoil your work and injure the true qi."
The work of sitting is not in how much you sit; / it all depends on refining qi and putting demons to flight;
So sweep all hindrances away in one clean cast, / and let no net of snares about your heart be cast.
If hindrances are not cleared, the afflictions gather fast; / if the net is not untied, how can one roam at leisure at last?
The highest principle is plainly handed down to you: / do not by dawdling make your own road rough and rue.
[Putting demons to flight] To rid oneself of delusive thoughts. [Roam at leisure] Leisurely and carefree.
[Dawdling] To drag and be slack.

When Master Chongyang had finished discoursing on the sitting work, he left the seat to rest, and the disciples each returned to their quarters; of this we say no more. It is further told that in Dou village of Qixia county in the prefecture of Dengzhou, Shandong, there was a man surnamed Qiu, named Chuji, whose courtesy name was Qifa. There were three brothers: the eldest was Qiming, the second Qixing, and their parents had died early. This Qiu Qifa, thanks to the care of his elder brothers and their wives, grew to manhood. He had studied a few years and could also compose poems, lyrics, songs, and rhapsodies. But he had no heart for fame and rank; his whole bent was toward quiet, and he would often sit alone the whole day through, speaking to no one. It seemed that in this he found something to his liking, yet no one knew why it was so. His brothers and their wives urged him again and again to study and seek fame, and he answered them, "Study is for the fathoming of principle; why should I covet fame?" When they wished to arrange a marriage for him, he firmly refused, saying, "Before a man is established, how can he let marriage bind and hobble him (
xiè bàn

, entangle and bind)?" His brothers and their wives, hearing his words were out of the common, did not dare press him hard, and let him have his way. Qiu Qifa would often say to people, "A man lives in the world: if he does not seek a path by which to get out, but all day contends for fame and covets profit, is greedy for wife and clingingly fond of children, then when impermanence comes, all things are empty. Other men think the affairs of the world are all real; in my eyes they are drifting clouds and morning dew, a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow."

One day he heard men say that at Ma Family Estate in Ninghai county there was a Master Wang Chongyang, a man of wide virtue and a great cultivator, and that several men from Qixia county were studying the Way there. Qiu Qifa had loved the Way all his life, and when he heard this he too wished to go and study it. He had not yet made it known to his brothers and their wives, and he feared they would not let him go, so he had no choice but to quietly put together a little traveling money, take a few changes of clothes, and slip away secretly from home, heading for Ninghai county.

Before many days he reached Ma Family Estate. That day it happened that Ma Danyang was on duty; he asked his purpose, and wrote his name in the register. Tan, Liu, Wang, Hao, and the rest all came to look him over, and said with one voice, glad at heart, "So young a man, and he can sincerely study the Way; truly this is rarely heard of." So saying, they led him to the thatched hut to pay his respects to Master Chongyang. Ma Danyang then told the master of his wish to study the Way. Master Chongyang looked him over, shook his head, and said, "This man has too many thoughts and is too clever; he cannot study the Way. Let him hurry home at once and not ruin himself." Qiu Qifa knelt and said, "This humble one has set his whole heart on the Way, with no second thought; I beg the master to take me in." Ma Danyang too pleaded on his behalf, but the master would not consent, saying, "It is not that I will not take him; this man's root of suffering is very heavy, and I fear that later he will not endure the trials, and will surely conceive the thought of retreat and regret. Better not to take him at all." Qiu Qifa would have pleaded again, but Master Chongyang had gone out of the thatched hut to look at the flowers.
